headline: Nepal's army drills into flooded hydropower tunnels as the flood toll passes 900
dek: Four bodies have been recovered from three mud-filled tunnels in Rasuwa district, and rescuers say oxygen has been delivered to some of the workers still underground. Nepal's disaster authority put the confirmed death toll at 939 on Monday; other counts published the same day give 903.
summary: Rescuers in Nepal are drilling into hydropower tunnels blocked by flood debris, six days after a Himalayan flash flood. Confirmed deaths have passed 900, and hundreds of workers remain unaccounted for.

follow_up.whats_new: The search has resumed and shifted underground: Nepal's army is now drilling into three mud-filled hydropower tunnels in Rasuwa district and has recovered four bodies from them, and rescuers say oxygen has been delivered to some workers still inside. Nepal's confirmed death toll has risen from more than 570 to 903-939 depending on the count, and the United Nations has published its first detailed assessment of humanitarian needs.

image.alt: A steep Himalayan river valley under heavy cloud, with a silt-laden river running through it

body.text: Nepal's army is drilling into hydropower tunnels choked with mud and debris in Rasuwa district, north of Kathmandu, in an attempt to reach workers who have been underground since a flash flood tore down the valley six days ago. Four bodies have been recovered from three tunnels, the army said in figures reported on Tuesday by ABC News in Australia. Rescuers descending roughly 15 metres into a tunnel at the Trishuli-3 project have delivered oxygen to some of those still inside, according to accounts published on Monday and Tuesday.

The flood struck the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river system on 26 August, destroying bridges, roads and a string of hydropower plants on one of the main routes between Nepal and Tibet. Searching was suspended on both sides of the border on Friday when lakes dammed by flood debris began to spill. It has since resumed, and the focus has moved from the riverbanks to the tunnels.

How many people are trapped is not settled, and the two published accounts do not describe the same thing. Nepal's army, quoted by Al Jazeera on Monday, said more than 900 people were believed to be trapped underground. Mohan Kumar Dangi, president of the Independent Power Producers' Association Nepal, told ABC News that at least 900 people were unaccounted for across twelve damaged hydropower projects in the Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, and that around 500 of those were believed to be inside tunnels. At the Upper Trishuli-1 project alone, Mr Dangi put the number missing at 576, of whom roughly 300 were thought to be in a tunnel. Those figures come from an industry body rather than from a government authority, and no reconciled official count has been published.
Our main focus is on opening the tunnels.
body.cite: Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal Army spokesman, via Al Jazeera

body.text: The tunnels are large — built to carry water to turbines, and wide enough to drive a truck through. Some workers made distress calls in the first hours after the flood. Whether contact has been maintained since is unclear from the accounts available, six days in.
It's a race for time, as people need food and water.
body.cite: Jakob Steiner, geoscientist at the University of Graz, via ABC News

body.text: The published death tolls diverge, and all of them are provisional. Nepal's disaster authority put the confirmed toll at 939 on Monday, with 3,925 people missing including 592 foreign nationals, in figures carried by ABC News. Al Jazeera, reporting earlier the same day, gave the same authority's toll as 903 with 4,247 missing. The United Nations spokesman, Stéphane Dujarric, also used 903 and more than 4,200 missing at Monday's briefing in New York, and said more than 10,000 people had been rescued, among them 252 foreign nationals. The higher death toll paired with a lower missing figure is consistent with bodies being identified rather than with a separate surge, but no authority has said so, and this wire could not establish which count is the more current.

On the Chinese side of the border, authorities have reported at least 16 deaths and 546 people missing, a figure that includes 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries. China has deployed more than 2,100 rescue workers, allocated 220 million yuan — about $33 million — for relief, and sent nine tunnel rescue specialists to Nepal, according to Al Jazeera. Australia's foreign minister, Penny Wong, said her government was urgently trying to establish the whereabouts of Australians in the area and held grave concerns for their safety.

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs has published its first detailed assessment of what the flood has left behind. It estimates that 65,000 people need emergency water, sanitation and hygiene support; that 2,600 children under five require treatment for severe malnutrition; and that 10,500 pregnant and breastfeeding women need nutrition assistance. Nineteen schools were damaged, nine of them destroyed outright and eight now sheltering displaced families. Mr Dujarric said more than 22,000 children need protection services and that 107 children may have been separated from those who care for them. Fifteen municipalities have declared a flood emergency, and the government has deployed more than 20,000 search and rescue personnel; Al Jazeera put the number of security personnel involved at close to 21,000.

The World Food Programme has dispatched nearly 80 tonnes of food, enough for about 9,200 people for fifteen days. UNICEF has moved therapeutic food for 500 severely malnourished children and mobilised fifteen emergency medical teams. Access remains the constraint: highways into the worst-hit areas are still blocked. Speaking about the disaster, the UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, said a warming climate driven by the burning of coal, oil and gas makes such tragedies more likely — a general statement about risk rather than an analysis of this flood, for which no formal attribution study has been published.

body.title: On the figures in this article
items: Every casualty and missing figure here is provisional and was rising or being revised at the time of writing.
Where two sources give different numbers from the same authority on the same day, both are reported above rather than one being chosen.
No individual victim is named in this article, and none of the sources used are relied on for identifying details.

uncertain: Whether Nepal's confirmed death toll on Monday was 903 or 939. Both are attributed to the same national disaster authority by different outlets on the same day, and neither outlet explains the gap.

What the figure of 'more than 900' trapped refers to. Nepal's army is quoted describing 900 people trapped underground, while the Independent Power Producers' Association describes 900 unaccounted for across twelve projects of whom about 500 are thought to be in tunnels. These may be the same estimate described differently, or two different estimates.
Whether rescuers are still in contact with any of the workers inside the tunnels. Distress calls were reported in the first hours; the current state of contact was not stated in the sources read.
How many people were inside the tunnels when the flood arrived. No figure from an operator or a government authority was found.
The condition of those to whom oxygen has reportedly been delivered, and how many of them there are.

The number of foreign nationals missing. Nepal's authority is reported as giving 592 and China's as 261 from 23 countries; whether these overlap, and whether the Nepali nationals reported missing in Tibet are counted in both, could not be established.
Whether ABC News's account is in part agency copy. The dispatch carries Australian government comment that suggests its own reporting, but its origin was not stated on the page.
The cause of the flood itself, which earlier coverage attributed to a suspected ice-and-rock avalanche across the border in Tibet, remains without a published technical finding.
